newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Berlin hopes veterans can fill hotel rooms.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Berlin hopes veterans can fill hotel rooms.

text.p: Berlin's flagging tourism industry, in decline since the Berlin Wall was brought down, is hoping an old ally will once again come to the city's aid with another kind of "airlift".

Berlin has launched a new campaign to attract U.S. veterans back for tours of the once-divided city and hopes to fill its empty hotel bedrooms with former soldiers by tapping into German-American ties of the last 50 years.

"Nostalgic Journeys", as the new programme is called, was inaugurated in Berlin with a corporate- and city-sponsored preview tour for 60 former GIs, veterans ' club members and travel agents focusing on tourism for retired soldiers.

One of the agencies involved, Berlin Tourism Marketing (BTM), is hoping to attract thousands of veterans who will be willing to pay $999 for one-week package tours in Berlin including a trip of memorials and museums, air fare and hotel room.
Organisers selected Americans as the first target group for the tours, which will begin in January 1997, but programmes for British and French veterans are expected to follow.

Americans fought with the conquering forces in two World Wars and were the driving force behind the 1948-49 airlift which supplied food to a Berlin blockaded by Soviet troops. Throughout the Cold War they kept watch for a feared Soviet attack that never came.
More than 500,000 soldiers wore an American uniform in Berlin between 1945 and 1994 and several million more Americans served in West Germany as members of NATO forces.
For the organisers of "Nostalgic Journeys," each veteran represents a potential tourist.

"Americans are the most important foreign visitor group in Berlin and in Germany in general," said Bernd Buhmann, BTM's spokesman. "The time they spent here was very emotional and important for all of us."
But with the disappearance in 1990 of the city's most popular attraction -- the Wall -- tourism has fallen off.
Berlin said an emotional farewell to Allied soldiers in 1994 with nearly 50 parades and festivals.
An "advance force" of retired soldiers to visit Berlin this month said they were amazed that the country which many of them had left while it was in ruins now welcomed them enthusiastically.

"It's ironic being here today. Fifty years ago we were shooting at each other and now we are friends, which is how it should be," said 73-year-old Jim Stone, who fought as a corporal with the 12th Armored Division.
Inspecting an exhibition on the airlift at the Allies Museum in Berlin, Stone said he looked forward to meeting German war veterans during his stay.
Others had retained painful memories which they hoped to come to terms with on their trip back to Germany.

"I thought I'd have a grudging feeling about the German people but after seeing the hospitality of these people, my thoughts have changed," said Stanley Wojtusik, 71, who was held as a prisoner-of-war for 5-1/2 months near Dresden in 1944.

"We came over here for this tour not as "ugly Americans' but as people with an open frame of mind," Wojtusik, president of the U.S. Veterans of the Battle of the Bulge WWII, told a reception at the Allies Museum.

"I thought I'd never come back to Germany after the war. I guess a lot has changed," said Tom Jones, 71. "Some of the memories this trip brings up are bad, of course, but I had a lot of good friends here and was lucky -- very few of them were killed in the war.
"I'm a little bit surprised," Jones said. "I didn't think they'd be so happy to see us, but the reception has been just wonderful."
